hero.caption: The two days that ended the age of wood, as the home front pictured it: the flat, single-turreted *Monitor* (Stars and Stripes) trades fire at point-blank range with the smoke-wreathed casemate *Virginia* in Hampton Roads. Currier & Ives rushed the print out the same year, crowning it "in which the little 'Monitor' whipped the 'Merrimac.'"
hero.credit: Currier & Ives · hand-colored lithograph · 1862 · The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Commons) · public domain (CC0; published 1862, pre-1929)

figs.caption: The plan its critics turned into a joke. J.B. Elliott's 1861 cartoon map drapes a giant green snake (the "anaconda") over the Southern coastline and down the Mississippi, squeezing the Confederacy exactly the way Winfield Scott intended. The sneer became the strategy's name, and the strategy held.
figs.credit: J.B. Elliott · cartoon map (lithograph) · 1861 · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (published 1861, pre-1929)
figs.heading: The snake nobody wanted

figs.caption: Gideon Welles, Lincoln's Secretary of the Navy, ran the industrial sprint that turned a 42-ship afterthought into the largest fleet on earth in four years. The whiskers earned him the nickname "Father Neptune."
figs.credit: Popular Graphic Arts · print · 1860s · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (published pre-1929)
figs.heading: A navy built from almost nothing

figs.caption: A blockade runner caught; most weren't. The fast Confederate runner *Hope* is run down by the Union steamer *Aeolus* off Wilmington in 1864. Long, low, and built for speed, runners like her slipped through the net five times out of six; the South's trade strangled anyway.
figs.credit: Harper's Weekly (S.M. Lane, engraver) · wood engraving · 1864 · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (published 1864, pre-1929)
figs.heading: The cat-and-mouse off Nassau

figs.caption: Stephen Mallory, the Confederate Navy secretary, did the math, found it hopeless, and bet everything on a technology that could make numbers irrelevant: "I regard the possession of an iron-armored ship as a matter of the first necessity."
figs.credit: Mathew Brady studio (Civil War Glass Negatives) · photograph · c. 1860–1865 · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (published pre-1929)
figs.heading: Mallory's gamble

figs.caption: Mallory's weapon under construction: the raised, burned hull of the steam frigate *Merrimack* in the Gosport dry dock, being rebuilt into the casemate ironclad CSS *Virginia*, a sloped iron box bolted onto a salvaged warship.
figs.credit: G.S. Richardson · photo-lithograph (after a wartime view) · 1906 print of an 1861–62 scene · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (published pre-1929)
figs.heading: Mallory's gamble

figs.caption: March 8, the worst day: the *Virginia* drives her iron ram into the sloop *Cumberland*, which "went down with all her Flags flying," gun crews working the cannon as the water climbed the deck. About 121 of her men drowned with her.
figs.credit: Currier & Ives (sketched by F. Newman) · lithograph · 1862 · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (published 1862, pre-1929)
figs.heading: March 8: the worst day

figs.caption: Flag Officer Franklin Buchanan, who took the *Virginia* into Hampton Roads on March 8, and, reportedly enraged at Union resistance, climbed onto his own exposed deck to fire back and caught a rifle bullet in the thigh, handing off command before the *Monitor* even arrived.
figs.credit: Civil War Glass Negatives (Brady studio) · photograph · c. 1860–1865 · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (published pre-1929)
figs.orientation: PORTRAIT (447 × 640) — small original; usable at modest display size, do not upscale.
figs.heading: March 8: the worst day

figs.caption: John Ericsson, the Swedish-born engineer behind the "cheesebox on a raft." His radical design (a nearly flush hull and a single revolving turret) reportedly packed 40 patentable inventions and got built in roughly a hundred days.
figs.credit: Charles D. Fredricks & Co. · carte-de-visite albumen print · 1861–1865 · Library of Congress, Liljenquist Collection (Commons) · public domain (published pre-1929)
figs.heading: A cheesebox on a raft

figs.caption: Lieutenant John Worden, who conned the *Monitor* into Hampton Roads in the dark on the night of March 8 and commanded her in the duel the next morning, until a shell burst against his pilothouse viewing slit and blinded him.
figs.credit: Mathew Brady · photograph · c. 1865 (restored by A. Cuerden) · Library of Congress (Commons) · public domain (Brady d. 1896; published pre-1929)
figs.orientation: LANDSCAPE (7500 × 5952) — restored full plate; faces are clear and centered.
figs.heading: A cheesebox on a raft

figs.caption: The only ship of its kind, photographed for the only time: the *Monitor*'s deck and dented iron turret on the James River in July 1862, four months after the duel. The scars in the armor are where the *Virginia*'s shot struck and skipped away.
figs.credit: James F. Gibson · photograph · July 1862 · Library of Congress, Civil War Glass Negatives (Commons) · public domain (published pre-1929)
figs.orientation: LANDSCAPE (858 × 682), near-square. Smaller original — display at moderate size; do not upscale.
figs.heading: March 9: the duel that changed everything
